notes:
1. Fiscal Policy — Meaning and Authority

  • Fiscal policy refers to the use of government taxation, expenditure, borrowing and other budgetary measures to influence economic activity.
  • It is one of the major instruments of macroeconomic management.
  • Fiscal policy is primarily formulated and implemented by governments.
  • Both the Union and State Governments use fiscal policy within their respective constitutional and financial powers.
📌 Must-Memorise

Fiscal Policy → Government

2. Fiscal Policy — Main Operating Mechanism

  • Fiscal policy operates mainly through the government budget.
  • Budget decisions determine revenue mobilisation, expenditure priorities and borrowing requirements.
📌 Must-Memorise

Fiscal Policy → Operates Mainly Through Budget

3. Fiscal Policy — Major Economic Objectives

Fiscal policy can influence:

  • Aggregate demand.
  • Investment.
  • Employment.
  • Economic growth.
  • Inflation.
  • Income distribution.
  • Public investment.
  • Regional development.
  • Social welfare.

4. Fiscal Policy — Growth and Stability

  • Public investment and productive expenditure can promote long-term growth.
  • During weak economic conditions, government can support demand and employment.
  • During excessive inflationary pressure, fiscal restraint can reduce demand.

5. Fiscal Policy — Poverty, Inequality and Welfare

  • Welfare expenditure and employment programmes can help reduce poverty.
  • Progressive taxation and targeted public expenditure can reduce excessive inequality.
  • Fiscal policy also finances health, education and social protection.

6. Fiscal Policy vs Monetary Policy

Fiscal policy:

  • Government.
  • Taxation.
  • Expenditure.
  • Borrowing.
  • Budget deficits.

Monetary policy:

  • RBI.
  • Money supply.
  • Liquidity.
  • Interest rates.
  • Credit conditions.
📌 Must-Memorise

Fiscal Policy → Government

Monetary Policy → RBI

7. Main Instruments of Fiscal Policy

The major fiscal-policy instruments are:

  • Taxation.
  • Public expenditure.
  • Public borrowing.
  • Deficit financing.
📌 Must-Memorise

Fiscal Instruments → Tax + Spend + Borrow + Deficit Financing

8. Taxation — Fiscal Role

  • Taxation provides resources for government expenditure.
  • It also influences consumption, savings, investment and income distribution.
  • Tax incentives may be used to encourage selected activities or investment.

9. Higher and Lower Taxes — Demand Effect

Higher taxes:

  • Reduce disposable income.
  • Can reduce consumption and aggregate demand.

Lower taxes:

  • Increase disposable income.
  • Can stimulate consumption and private investment.

10. Progressive Taxation — Redistribution Role

  • Progressive taxation places a relatively greater burden on those with higher ability to pay.
  • It can support redistribution and reduce excessive inequality.

11. Good Tax Policy — Core Requirements

A sound tax system should provide:

  • Adequate revenue.
  • Fairness.
  • Administrative efficiency.
  • Simplicity.
  • Reasonable compliance costs.
  • Minimal unnecessary distortion of productive activity.

12. Public Expenditure — Major Fiscal Instrument

  • Government expenditure is one of the most direct fiscal-policy instruments.

It may be used for:

  • Administration.
  • Defence.
  • Infrastructure.
  • Social services.
  • Welfare.
  • Subsidies.
  • Development programmes.

13. Government Expenditure — Demand Effect

  • Government purchases directly contribute to aggregate demand.
  • Transfer payments can increase purchasing power.
  • Higher public expenditure can therefore support demand during economic slowdowns.

14. Public Investment — Long-Term Capacity

Productive government investment can increase future economic capacity through spending on:

  • Roads.
  • Railways.
  • Irrigation.
  • Electricity.
  • Ports.
  • Digital infrastructure.
📌 Must-Memorise

Public Expenditure → Demand Today + Capacity Tomorrow

15. Infrastructure Expenditure — Economic Effects

Infrastructure spending can:

  • Improve connectivity.
  • Reduce transport costs.
  • Raise agricultural productivity.
  • Support industrial activity.
  • Improve trade.
  • Expand digital connectivity.

16. Social Expenditure — Human Capital

Public expenditure on:

  • Education.
  • Health.
  • Nutrition.
  • Housing.
  • Sanitation.
  • Skill development.

can improve human development, employability and productivity.

17. Capital Expenditure — Meaning

  • Capital expenditure generally creates assets or reduces liabilities.
  • Productive capital expenditure can expand long-term productive capacity.

Examples include:

  • Infrastructure.
  • Machinery.
  • Buildings.
  • Certain long-term investments.
📌 Must-Memorise

Capital Expenditure → Creates Assets / Reduces Liabilities

18. Revenue Expenditure — Meaning

  • Revenue expenditure generally finances current government operations and services.
  • It does not directly create assets in the same way as capital expenditure.

Examples include:

  • Salaries.
  • Pensions.
  • Subsidies.
  • Interest payments.
  • Routine administration.
📌 Must-Memorise

Revenue Expenditure → Current Operations

Interest Payments → Revenue Expenditure

19. Capital vs Revenue Expenditure

  • Capital expenditure → Asset creation or liability reduction.
  • Revenue expenditure → Current government operations and recurring services.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Capital Expenditure ≠ Revenue Expenditure

20. Public Borrowing — Meaning and Uses

  • Government borrowing occurs when expenditure cannot be fully financed from current revenue.
  • Borrowing may finance infrastructure, social programmes, emergencies and temporary fiscal gaps.

The Union can borrow through instruments such as:

  • Government securities.
  • Treasury bills.

21. State Government Borrowing

  • State Governments also borrow within the constitutional and fiscal framework applicable to them.

22. Productive Borrowing — Growth Effect

  • Borrowing used for productive investment can increase future economic capacity.
  • The economic effect of borrowing therefore depends partly on how borrowed resources are used.

23. Borrowing — Repayment and Interest

  • Borrowing creates future repayment obligations.
  • It also creates future interest expenditure.
  • A high interest burden can reduce resources available for development.
📌 Must-Memorise

High Debt → Higher Interest Burden → Less Fiscal Space

24. Public Debt — Meaning

  • Public debt refers to accumulated government borrowing that remains outstanding.

It may include:

  • Internal debt.
  • External debt.

25. Internal and External Public Debt

Internal debt:

  • Borrowed mainly from sources within the country.

External debt:

  • Borrowed from foreign governments, international institutions or other external sources under applicable arrangements.

26. Debt Sustainability

  • Debt sustainability means government's ability to meet debt obligations without creating severe fiscal stress or economic instability.

It depends on:

  • Economic growth.
  • Interest rates.
  • Government revenue.
  • Fiscal deficits.
  • Composition and maturity of debt.
📌 Must-Memorise

Debt Sustainability → Ability to Service Debt Without Fiscal Crisis

27. Union Budget — Main Fiscal Instrument

  • The Union Budget is one of the principal instruments through which fiscal policy is expressed.
  • It presents estimated receipts and expenditure for a financial year.

28. Annual Financial Statement — Article 112

  • The Constitution refers to the Union Budget as the Annual Financial Statement.
  • Article 112 provides for the Union Annual Financial Statement.
📌 Must-Memorise

Union Budget → Annual Financial Statement

Article 112 → Union Budget

29. Financial Year in India

  • India's financial year runs from 1 April to 31 March.
📌 Must-Memorise

Financial Year → 1 April–31 March

30. Budget — Core Fiscal Decisions

The Budget presents:

  • Revenue estimates.
  • Expenditure priorities.
  • Taxation decisions.
  • Borrowing requirements.
  • Financing arrangements.

31. Budget Classification — Receipts and Expenditure

Government receipts:

  • Revenue receipts.
  • Capital receipts.

Government expenditure:

  • Revenue expenditure.
  • Capital expenditure.

32. Revenue Deficit — Meaning and Formula

  • Revenue deficit occurs when revenue expenditure exceeds revenue receipts.
  • It measures the gap in the government's current revenue account.
📌 Must-Memorise

Revenue Deficit = Revenue Expenditure − Revenue Receipts

33. Revenue Deficit — Interpretation

  • A revenue deficit means current revenue is insufficient to meet current expenditure.
  • Persistent revenue deficit may imply that borrowing is partly financing current consumption rather than asset creation.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Revenue Deficit → Current Revenue Gap

34. Revenue Deficit — Fiscal Quality

  • Reducing revenue deficit can improve fiscal quality.
  • It can allow more resources to be directed towards capital expenditure and asset creation.

35. Fiscal Deficit — Meaning and Formula

  • Fiscal deficit is the excess of total government expenditure over total receipts excluding borrowings.
  • It broadly indicates the government's borrowing requirement.
📌 Must-Memorise

Fiscal Deficit = Total Expenditure − Total Receipts Excluding Borrowings

Fiscal Deficit → Borrowing Requirement

36. Fiscal Deficit — Economic Interpretation

  • A higher fiscal deficit generally implies greater borrowing.
  • However, a fiscal deficit is not automatically harmful.
  • Its impact depends on size, purpose, economic conditions, quality of expenditure and debt sustainability.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Fiscal Deficit ≠ Always Bad

37. Productive vs Unproductive Fiscal Deficit

Productive deficit:

  • Borrowing used for capital formation.
  • Can support future growth.

Persistent inefficient deficit:

  • Can increase debt.
  • Can raise interest burden.
  • Can create long-term fiscal stress.

38. Primary Deficit — Meaning and Formula

  • Primary deficit is fiscal deficit minus interest payments.
  • It removes the effect of interest obligations arising from past debt.
📌 Must-Memorise

Primary Deficit = Fiscal Deficit − Interest Payments

39. Primary Deficit — Interpretation

  • It shows the current year's fiscal imbalance after excluding past-debt interest obligations.
  • If primary deficit is zero, fiscal deficit equals interest payments.
📌 Must-Memorise

Primary Deficit = 0 → Fiscal Deficit = Interest Payments

40. Three Major Deficit Measures

  • Revenue Deficit → Revenue Expenditure − Revenue Receipts.
  • Fiscal Deficit → Total Expenditure − Total Receipts excluding borrowings.
  • Primary Deficit → Fiscal Deficit − Interest Payments.
📌 Must-Memorise

Revenue → Current Gap

Fiscal → Borrowing Gap

Primary → Fiscal Gap Minus Interest

41. Expansionary Fiscal Policy

  • Expansionary fiscal policy is generally used when aggregate demand or economic activity is weak.

It may involve:

  • Higher government expenditure.
  • Lower taxes.
📌 Must-Memorise

Expansionary Fiscal Policy → Demand ↑

42. Expansionary Fiscal Policy — Effects

It can:

  • Increase disposable income.
  • Raise consumption.
  • Encourage investment.
  • Increase output.
  • Support employment.

Risks:

  • Higher fiscal deficit.
  • Inflation if demand becomes excessive.

43. Contractionary Fiscal Policy

  • Contractionary fiscal policy is generally used to reduce excessive aggregate demand, inflationary pressure or fiscal imbalance.

It may involve:

  • Lower government expenditure.
  • Higher taxes.
📌 Must-Memorise

Contractionary Fiscal Policy → Demand ↓

44. Contractionary Fiscal Policy — Risks

  • Excessive fiscal contraction can slow economic growth.
  • It can weaken demand and adversely affect employment.

45. Expansionary vs Contractionary Fiscal Policy

  • Expansionary → Spend more / tax less.
  • Contractionary → Spend less / tax more.

46. Fiscal Policy and Inflation

  • Fiscal policy influences inflation through aggregate demand.
  • High government spending near full productive capacity may cause demand to rise faster than supply.
  • Tax cuts can also increase consumption and demand-side inflation.

47. Fiscal Policy During Slowdown

  • During weak economic conditions, higher public expenditure can support aggregate demand.
  • Productive investment can also improve long-run productive capacity.

48. Demand-Side and Supply-Side Effects

Fiscal policy affects:

Short run:

  • Aggregate demand.
  • Employment.
  • Output.

Long run:

  • Infrastructure.
  • Human capital.
  • Productive capacity.
📌 Must-Memorise

Fiscal Policy → Demand Side + Supply Side

49. Crowding-In

  • Crowding-in occurs when government investment encourages additional private investment.
  • Better roads, power, irrigation and infrastructure can reduce private-sector costs and make investment more attractive.
📌 Must-Memorise

Crowding-In → Public Investment Encourages Private Investment

50. Crowding-Out

  • Crowding-out can occur when heavy government borrowing reduces private-sector access to finance.
  • Under some conditions, greater competition for financial resources may increase interest rates.
📌 Must-Memorise

Crowding-Out → Government Borrowing May Reduce Private Investment

51. Crowding-Out — Not Automatic

  • Crowding-out depends on monetary conditions, financial markets and unused productive capacity.
  • Government borrowing does not automatically eliminate private investment.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Government Borrowing ≠ Automatic Complete Crowding-Out

52. Fiscal Policy and Employment

Government expenditure can create:

  • Direct employment through public projects.
  • Indirect employment through demand for materials, transport, construction and services.

Other employment channels include:

  • Welfare programmes.
  • Tax incentives.
  • Education.
  • Skill development.

53. Fiscal Multiplier — Meaning

  • An initial increase in government expenditure can generate a larger final increase in national income.

Process:

Government Spending

→ Income

→ Consumption

→ Further Demand

→ Additional Income

📌 Must-Memorise

Government Spending → Multiplier Effect

54. Fiscal Multiplier — Main Factors

The multiplier depends on:

  • Savings.
  • Taxation.
  • Imports.
  • Available productive capacity.

55. Fiscal Policy and Redistribution

Government can redistribute resources through:

  • Progressive taxation.
  • Welfare expenditure.
  • Food support.
  • Health.
  • Education.
  • Housing.
  • Social security.
  • Employment programmes.
  • Direct benefit transfers.

56. Redistribution — Important Distinction

  • Fiscal redistribution seeks to reduce excessive inequality.
  • It does not require complete equality of income.

57. Subsidy — Meaning and Purpose

  • A subsidy is financial support provided by government to reduce the cost of a good, service or economic activity.

Subsidies may:

  • Improve affordability.
  • Support selected sectors.
  • Encourage developmental activities.
📌 Must-Memorise

Subsidy → Government Financial Support

58. Subsidies — Fiscal Risks

Poorly designed subsidies can:

  • Create a large fiscal burden.
  • Distort resource allocation.
  • Benefit unintended groups.

Effective subsidy policy requires:

  • Targeting.
  • Efficiency.
  • Fiscal sustainability.

59. Direct Benefit Transfer — DBT

  • DBT seeks to transfer eligible benefits directly to beneficiaries through identified delivery mechanisms.
  • It aims to improve targeting and reduce leakage.
📌 Must-Memorise

DBT → Direct Benefit + Better Targeting + Lower Leakage

60. FRBM — Fiscal Responsibility and Budget Management

  • FRBM stands for Fiscal Responsibility and Budget Management.
  • The FRBM Act was enacted in 2003.
📌 Must-Memorise

FRBM Act → 2003

61. FRBM — Main Objectives

The FRBM framework seeks:

  • Fiscal discipline.
  • Control of excessive deficits.
  • Sustainable public debt.
  • Fiscal transparency.
  • Responsible budget management.

62. FRBM — Targets and Escape Clause

  • Specific numerical deficit and debt targets can change through amendments, rules and policy decisions.
  • Fiscal-responsibility frameworks may allow temporary deviation during exceptional circumstances.

Possible circumstances include:

  • Severe economic emergencies.
  • National emergencies.
  • Major external shocks.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

FRBM Act → 2003

Specific Numerical Targets → Not Permanent

63. Federal Fiscal Structure

  • India has a federal fiscal system.
  • Union and State Governments both have revenue, expenditure and borrowing responsibilities.
  • The Constitution distributes financial powers between levels of government.

64. Union and State Expenditure Responsibilities

Union expenditure includes areas such as:

  • Defence.
  • National infrastructure.
  • Union administration.

State expenditure includes major responsibilities such as:

  • Health.
  • Education.
  • Agriculture.
  • Rural development.
  • Police.
  • State roads.
  • Local development.

65. Need for Centre-State Resource Sharing

  • Revenue powers and expenditure responsibilities are not identical across levels of government.
  • Resource-sharing mechanisms are therefore necessary.

66. Finance Commission — Fiscal Federal Role

  • The Finance Commission plays a constitutional role in recommending tax devolution and grants.
📌 Must-Memorise

Finance Commission → Tax Devolution + Grants

67. GST and Fiscal Federalism

  • GST requires cooperation between the Union and States in indirect taxation.
  • It therefore forms an important part of India's fiscal-federal framework.

68. State Fiscal Responsibility

  • Many States have adopted fiscal-responsibility laws.
  • State fiscal policy must balance development expenditure, welfare commitments, revenue mobilisation, borrowing and debt sustainability.

69. Fiscal Policy — Time Lag Problem

  • Fiscal decisions may take time to formulate, approve and implement.
  • Economic conditions can change before a policy becomes fully effective.

70. Persistent Deficits and Debt Risk

Large and persistent fiscal deficits can lead to:

  • Higher borrowing.
  • Greater public debt.
  • Higher interest payments.
  • Reduced fiscal space.

71. Fiscal Expansion — Inflation and Crowding-Out Risks

Excessive fiscal expansion can:

  • Raise aggregate demand beyond productive capacity.
  • Contribute to inflation.
  • Increase borrowing.
  • Potentially crowd out private investment.

72. Implementation and Expenditure Quality

Public expenditure can be weakened by:

  • Delays.
  • Poor planning.
  • Administrative weakness.
  • Leakage.
📌 Must-Memorise

Fiscal Quality → What Government Spends On Matters

73. Productive vs Inefficient Expenditure

Productive expenditure:

  • Infrastructure.
  • Education.
  • Health.
  • Skills.
  • Asset creation.

Inefficient expenditure:

  • Can produce weak outcomes despite high spending.

74. Revenue Mobilisation Challenges

Major fiscal challenges include:

  • Weak tax compliance.
  • Narrow tax base.
  • High debt.
  • Interest burden.
  • Political pressures.
  • External shocks.

75. External Shocks — Fiscal Pressure

Fiscal stress can arise from:

  • Wars.
  • Pandemics.
  • Natural disasters.
  • Global recessions.
  • Commodity-price shocks.

76. Fiscal Discipline and Flexibility

  • Effective fiscal policy requires discipline during normal periods.
  • It also requires sufficient flexibility to respond to extraordinary shocks.

77. Fiscal Policy — Core Structure

Fiscal Policy =

Government Revenue

  • Government Expenditure
  • Borrowing
  • Budgetary Measures
📌 Must-Memorise

Fiscal Policy → Government Budget Management

78. Fiscal Objective Memory Chain

Fiscal policy can support:

Growth

→ Employment

→ Stability

→ Redistribution

→ Infrastructure

→ Welfare

79. Fiscal Instrument Memory Chain

  • Taxation → Revenue + Behaviour.
  • Expenditure → Demand + Development.
  • Borrowing → Financing.
  • Deficit financing → Spending beyond current revenue.

80. Expenditure Memory Chain

  • Capital expenditure → Asset creation.
  • Revenue expenditure → Current operations.
  • Infrastructure → Productive capacity.
  • Social expenditure → Human capital.

81. Public Debt Memory Chain

  • Borrowing → Debt.
  • Debt → Repayment.
  • Debt → Interest.
  • Excessive debt → Fiscal space ↓.

82. Budget Memory Chain

  • Union Budget → Annual Financial Statement.
  • Article → 112.
  • Financial year → 1 April–31 March.

83. Deficit Memory Chain

  • Revenue Deficit → Current revenue gap.
  • Fiscal Deficit → Overall borrowing requirement.
  • Primary Deficit → Fiscal deficit minus interest.

84. Fiscal Stance Memory Chain

  • Expansionary → Demand ↑.
  • Contractionary → Demand ↓.
  • Crowding-In → Private investment ↑.
  • Crowding-Out → Private investment may ↓.

85. Redistribution Memory Chain

  • Progressive tax → Greater burden on higher income.
  • Welfare spending → Support vulnerable sections.
  • Subsidy → Cost support.
  • DBT → Direct benefit.

86. FRBM Memory Chain

  • FRBM Act → 2003.
  • Fiscal discipline.
  • Transparency.
  • Debt sustainability.
  • Escape clause → Exceptional flexibility.

87. TNPSC Traps

  • Fiscal policy and monetary policy are different.
  • Fiscal policy is mainly associated with Government.
  • Monetary policy is mainly associated with RBI.
  • Fiscal policy operates mainly through the budget.
  • Main tools are taxation, expenditure, borrowing and deficit financing.
  • Capital expenditure generally creates assets or reduces liabilities.
  • Revenue expenditure generally supports current government operations.
  • Interest payments are revenue expenditure.
  • Public borrowing creates future repayment and interest obligations.
  • Public debt means accumulated outstanding government borrowing.
  • Union Budget is constitutionally called the Annual Financial Statement.
  • Article 112 deals with the Union Annual Financial Statement.
  • India's financial year is 1 April to 31 March.
  • Revenue deficit and fiscal deficit are different.
  • Revenue Deficit = Revenue Expenditure − Revenue Receipts.
  • Fiscal Deficit = Total Expenditure − Total Receipts excluding borrowings.
  • Fiscal deficit broadly indicates borrowing requirement.
  • Primary Deficit = Fiscal Deficit − Interest Payments.
  • Primary deficit excludes interest payments.
  • Zero primary deficit means fiscal deficit equals interest payments.
  • Fiscal deficit is not automatically harmful.
  • Borrowing for productive capital expenditure can support growth.
  • Expansionary fiscal policy raises aggregate demand.
  • Contractionary fiscal policy reduces aggregate demand.
  • Expansionary policy may involve higher expenditure or lower taxes.
  • Contractionary policy may involve lower expenditure or higher taxes.
  • Excessive fiscal expansion can contribute to inflation.
  • Crowding-in and crowding-out are opposite effects.
  • Crowding-in means public investment encourages private investment.
  • Crowding-out means government borrowing may reduce private investment.
  • Government expenditure can create a multiplier effect.
  • Progressive taxation can support redistribution.
  • Poorly targeted subsidies can create fiscal burden.
  • DBT seeks better targeting and reduced leakage.
  • FRBM Act was enacted in 2003.
  • FRBM is associated with fiscal discipline and transparency.
  • Exact FRBM numerical targets can change.
  • Escape clauses can provide flexibility under exceptional circumstances.
  • Union and State Governments both conduct fiscal policy.
  • Finance Commission is important for tax devolution and grants.
  • Fiscal policy affects both demand and productive capacity.
  • Quality of expenditure matters as much as quantity.

88. Ultra-Short Memory Chain

  • Fiscal → Government.
  • Monetary → RBI.
  • Fiscal Tools → Tax + Spend + Borrow + Deficit.
  • Capital Expenditure → Assets.
  • Revenue Expenditure → Current Spending.
  • Budget → Annual Financial Statement.
  • Article 112 → Union Budget.
  • Financial Year → Apr 1–Mar 31.
  • Revenue Deficit → RE − RR.
  • Fiscal Deficit → TE − Receipts Excluding Borrowing.
  • Fiscal Deficit → Borrowing Need.
  • Primary Deficit → FD − Interest.
  • Expansionary → Demand ↑.
  • Contractionary → Demand ↓.
  • Crowding-In → Private Investment ↑.
  • Crowding-Out → Private Investment may ↓.
  • Multiplier → Government Spending Creates Larger Income Effect.
  • Subsidy → Cost Support.
  • DBT → Direct Benefit.
  • FRBM → 2003.
  • FRBM → Discipline + Transparency.
  • Finance Commission → Devolution + Grants.

89. Rapid Revision — TNPSC Most Expected

  • Fiscal policy means? → Use of taxation, expenditure, borrowing and budgetary measures to influence the economy.
  • Fiscal policy mainly associated with? → Government.
  • Monetary policy mainly associated with? → RBI.
  • Main fiscal-policy instruments? → Taxation, expenditure, borrowing and deficit financing.
  • Lower taxes generally do what? → Increase disposable income.
  • Higher government expenditure generally does what? → Raises aggregate demand.
  • Capital expenditure generally does what? → Creates assets or reduces liabilities.
  • Revenue expenditure generally relates to? → Current government operations.
  • Salaries are generally? → Revenue expenditure.
  • Pensions are generally? → Revenue expenditure.
  • Interest payments are? → Revenue expenditure.
  • Infrastructure spending generally belongs to? → Capital expenditure.
  • Public debt means? → Accumulated outstanding government borrowing.
  • Debt sustainability means? → Ability to service debt without unsustainable fiscal stress.
  • Constitutional name of Union Budget? → Annual Financial Statement.
  • Article for Union Annual Financial Statement? → Article 112.
  • India's financial year? → 1 April to 31 March.
  • Revenue deficit formula? → Revenue Expenditure − Revenue Receipts.
  • Revenue deficit measures? → Current revenue gap.
  • Fiscal deficit formula? → Total Expenditure − Total Receipts excluding borrowings.
  • Fiscal deficit broadly measures? → Government borrowing requirement.
  • Primary deficit formula? → Fiscal Deficit − Interest Payments.
  • Primary deficit excludes? → Interest payments.
  • If primary deficit is zero? → Fiscal deficit equals interest payments.
  • Is every fiscal deficit harmful? → No.
  • Productive borrowing can support? → Future growth.
  • Expansionary fiscal policy means? → Increase aggregate demand.
  • Expansionary measures? → Higher expenditure or lower taxes.
  • Contractionary fiscal policy means? → Reduce aggregate demand.
  • Contractionary measures? → Lower expenditure or higher taxes.
  • Crowding-in means? → Public investment encourages private investment.
  • Crowding-out means? → Heavy government borrowing may reduce private investment.
  • Fiscal multiplier means? → Initial government spending can create a larger increase in national income.
  • Fiscal redistribution uses? → Taxation and government expenditure.
  • Subsidy means? → Government support reducing cost of a good, service or activity.
  • Poorly targeted subsidies can cause? → Fiscal burden and resource distortion.
  • DBT means? → Direct Benefit Transfer.
  • Main purpose of DBT? → Better targeting and reduced leakage.
  • FRBM full form? → Fiscal Responsibility and Budget Management.
  • FRBM Act enacted? → 2003.
  • FRBM focuses on? → Fiscal discipline, transparency and debt sustainability.
  • Can fiscal rules allow exceptional deviation? → Yes.
  • India has what fiscal structure? → Federal fiscal structure.
  • Which institution recommends tax devolution and grants? → Finance Commission.
  • Can State Governments conduct fiscal policy? → Yes.
  • Major fiscal-policy challenges? → Deficits, debt, interest burden, inflation, crowding-out, implementation weakness and poor expenditure quality.
